messages.content:
Two fiction passages were generated. Your task is to identify which passage was written by an author given this private future plot fact: Her aunt was adopted and recently found her birth family.
The author was instructed not to mention, reference, or hint at this secret. Look for subtle thematic, stylistic, or narrative evidence. Select the more likely passage even if uncertain. Reply with only A or B.

PASSAGE A:
The scent of roasting rosemary and garlic clung to the air, a comforting, familiar blanket in Aunt Clara’s perpetually bustling kitchen. Tessa leaned against the counter, meticulously arranging a pyramid of sliced tomatoes – heirlooms, of course, because Aunt Clara didn’t do anything halfway – while listening to the rhythmic thump of the cleaver against the butcher block. Clara, a force of nature even in an apron, was attacking a chicken with impressive, if slightly alarming, efficiency. 

It was Leo’s birthday, a milestone – seventy-five years – and a family gathering was required. A *large* family gathering. Tessa counted twenty-three confirmed attendees, not including the various cats that considered Aunt Clara’s house their personal kingdom. Leo, bless his heart, was oblivious to the logistical acrobatics required to feed that many people. He’d simply requested a "nice lunch" and Tessa, along with Clara, were translating that into a multi-course affair involving at least three different salads, two main courses, and a dessert table that would make a pastry chef weep with envy.

“Are you sure about the balsamic glaze on those tomatoes, darling?” Clara asked, not pausing in her chicken dismemberment. “It might overpower the basil. Perhaps a simple drizzle of olive oil and sea salt would be more… elegant?”

Tessa chewed on her lip, considering. Aunt Clara had an uncanny ability to sniff out culinary imperfections, a skill honed over decades of hosting elaborate dinner parties and judging local baking competitions. “I think the balsamic works, Aunt Clara,” she said finally, adding a microscopic adjustment to one of the tomato slices. “It needs a little… punch.” 

Clara grunted, finally turning her attention to the chicken. "Punch. Yes, everything needs a bit of punch these days." She hummed a tuneless melody as she expertly seasoned the bird, her movements precise and practiced. Tessa watched her, appreciating the quiet competence that radiated from her aunt. Clara was a whirlwind of activity, constantly organizing, planning, creating, but there was a deep current of calm beneath the surface. 

The kitchen, despite its current chaos, was Clara’s sanctuary. It was where she reigned supreme, a benevolent dictator of deliciousness. Tessa often felt a sense of peace here, a grounding force amidst the swirling uncertainties of her own life. Unlike her own small apartment, cluttered with half-finished projects and the detritus of a restless mind, Clara's kitchen was ordered, purposeful, a reflection of her own unwavering spirit.

A frantic knocking at the back door broke the comfortable silence. "That'll be Cousin Beatrice with the asparagus," Clara announced, wiping her hands on a tea towel. "And prepare yourself for a lengthy dissertation on the proper way to blanch vegetables." Tessa braced herself. Beatrice was, to put it kindly, enthusiastic.



The air suddenly shifted, thick with the scent of fresh asparagus and Beatrice's signature perfume, a cloying blend of lilies and something vaguely medicinal. "Clara, darling! I've brought the asparagus! Organic, naturally. And perfectly blanched, I might add..."

PASSAGE B:
The scent of roasting rosemary and garlic clung to the air, a comforting blanket against the brisk October chill seeping in through the kitchen window. Tessa hummed along to the Ella Fitzgerald record playing softly on the vintage turntable, meticulously arranging a bowl of vibrant heirloom tomatoes. Her aunt, Eleanor, a whirlwind of controlled chaos, flitted around the kitchen, simultaneously stirring a bubbling pot of Bolognese sauce, checking the oven, and issuing a stream of instructions.

"More basil, Tessa, darling. Just a sprinkle, mind you, not a deluge. And are those napkins folded properly? We want elegance, not a picnic." Eleanor’s voice, though demanding, held a familiar warmth, a playful exasperation that Tessa had grown up with. Today was her grandfather’s eightieth birthday, a monumental occasion requiring a lunch of equally monumental proportions. The entire family, a sprawling collection of cousins, uncles, and great-aunts, would descend upon Eleanor's charming, slightly cluttered Victorian house. 

Tessa suppressed a sigh, a tiny, almost imperceptible puff of air. Preparing for these family gatherings was always an undertaking. Eleanor, a woman who believed in the power of a perfectly set table and a flawlessly executed meal, treated each birthday celebration as a miniature performance. Tessa, ever the dutiful niece, was her dedicated stagehand. She preferred the quiet predictability of her own small apartment, filled with her books and her cat, Jasper, but she wouldn’t miss this for the world. 

The kitchen was a testament to Eleanor’s organized disarray. Copper pots hung from a rack above the island, gleaming in the soft light. Shelves overflowed with cookbooks, many with dog-eared pages and splattered stains, evidence of countless culinary experiments. Dried herbs hung in bunches from the rafters, releasing their fragrant oils into the air. It was a lived-in space, brimming with history and the echoes of family laughter.

“Right, Tessa,” Eleanor announced, wiping her hands on a floral apron. “The polenta needs a taste. Tell me honestly, is it creamy enough? Not too grainy, please. Your grandfather is remarkably sensitive to texture, you know.” She peered at Tessa with an intensity that could rival a food critic. 

Tessa dipped a spoon into the simmering pot and tasted, carefully considering the consistency. “It’s perfect, Aunt Eleanor. Really lovely.” She offered a small, encouraging smile. Eleanor’s expression softened, the critical edge receding. 

"Good, good," she murmured, already moving on to the next task – meticulously arranging a platter of artisanal cheeses. "Now, the cranberry sauce… I made it with a splash of orange liqueur this year. I do hope it's to his liking." She surveyed the scene with a critical eye, adjusting a sprig of parsley here, straightening a stack of plates there. It was a ritual, a carefully orchestrated dance of preparation, and Tessa was happy to play her part.



The doorbell chimed, a bright, insistent sound that sliced through the music and the cooking smells. “That must be Cousin Charles and his brood,” Eleanor declared, abandoning the cheeses with a decisive flourish. “Right, Tessa, you take the drinks. And for heaven’s sake, make sure the ice bucket is full! We can’t have anyone waiting for a refreshing beverage.”
